We shall have occasion to return to this point in discussing his mystical Tales, as well as the mysterious country where the Hidden Imam resides—the Green Island and other such places (see Book VII).

Thus there is a succession of Easts. As the human being rises out of the Western exile, one East after another dawns before the soul, from world to world, in a “hieratic ascent” through successive mornings and illuminations. This is istishrâq, literally the “quest for the East.” The mostashriq is the mystical pilgrim “in search of the East.” There is a certain humor in the fact that modern Arabic uses this very word for scholars called Orientalists. The vocabulary of Ishrâq might confront such scholars with obligations they had never expected.

The “quest for the East” undertaken by the Ishrâqîyûn is a pilgrimage through the Easts that dawn from vision to vision, from ecstasy to ecstasy. Each ecstasy is a “lesser death,” until the final ecstasy arrives: the “greater death” to the “Western” world, when the soul rises definitively into its Heaven. This is not merely a growing intellectual certainty, but a spiritual union with the successive ranks of a hierarchy of beings of Light, up to the threshold of all thresholds. It is deeply significant that Sohrawardî made Hermes the first hero of these ecstatic encounters with the Last Things, or this ecstatic eschatology (see Chapter VI): the archetypal hero of the pilgrimage leading back to the East.

We shall also see that Sohrawardî's Hermeticism contributes to the theme of the Quest. Unfortunately, this contribution has been overlooked by recent studies that have traced the Hermetic origins of the Quest for the Grail as presented in Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parsifal.

“Eastern knowledge” (’ilm ishrâqî) is therefore both the goal and the means of the pilgrim's Quest toward the East. That is because it is not theoretical knowledge but a transformation of being. It is knowledge that is real Presence, literally knowledge by presence (’ilm hozûrî). As such, it stands opposed to representational knowledge, the kind assumed by the Peripatetic theory of knowledge. In that theory, knowledge reaches its object only through an intervening form of knowing, which is not the being of the object itself but a representation of that being (’ilm sûrî).

Even before composing his great work, Sohrawardî had described “Eastern” knowledge in his Book of Elucidations. He did so by recounting a dream—or, more precisely, a visionary conversation that took place in the state between waking and sleep. At that time, he tells us, he was obsessed with the problem of Knowledge. He meditated upon it incessantly but remained overwhelmed by difficulties, unable to glimpse a solution. Then, one night, he suddenly felt himself enveloped in great joy and radiant light. Gradually, a human figure took shape before him. He studied it attentively and soon recognized the Primus Magister, Aristotle, appearing in a form of astonishing beauty. In another of his books, Sohrawardî would refer back to this conversation and specify that it had taken place in Jâbarsâ, one of the cities of the intermediate East, the “eighth climate.” That is the imaginal world discussed above; this one example alone would be enough to show that our understanding of the worlds cannot dispense with it.

Is there a touch of humor in the Platonist language spoken by Aristotle in this vision? Or does it simply reflect the conviction that the author of the Theology—in reality, an adaptation of Plotinus's writings—had always been a Platonist in his inner teaching, and that only his successors were responsible for Peripatetic philosophy? At the end of their conversation, Sohrawardî asks Aristotle whether the philosophers of Islam, Fârâbî and Avicenna, have come close to Plato's rank. Aristotle replies: “Not even one degree in a thousand!”

Sohrawardî then turns his thoughts to Abû Yazîd Bastâmî and Sahl Tostarî, two Sufi masters whose names have already appeared in our genealogy of the Ishrâqîyûn. Bastâmî transmitted the spiritual leaven of the Khosrawânîyûn, while Tostarî transmitted that of the Pythagoreans. Aristotle reads the visionary's thoughts and declares, joyfully and with approval: “Yes, those are the philosophers and the theosophers in the true sense (al-falâsifa wa’l-hokamâ haqîqan). They did not content themselves with ordinary knowledge. They went beyond it and attained knowledge by presence, knowledge through union. They began where we ourselves began, and they spoke the truths that we ourselves spoke.” “Then,” the author continues, “the Sage left me, and I remained weeping over our separation. Ah, what grief and tears over this wretched condition!”

Unfortunately, we can give only a few indications of this conversation, whose narrative extends over several pages and is further enlarged by the commentators. The visionary lays his difficulties before the philosopher, whose first reply is: “Return to yourself, and the difficulty will be resolved for you.” This is the starting point, the very starting point recalled, as we have just read, at the end of the conversation. The entire exchange is, in essence, a progressive initiation into self-knowledge as something inherent in, and necessary to, all knowledge.

The initiation seeks to awaken the soul to a knowing that is neither the product of abstraction nor a representation of its object: a knowing that does not require the intervention of a form or species, a mental likeness. No: this act of Knowing is not something added to the knowing subject. It is the subject's very essence, the essence of the soul itself, of personal, existing subjectivity (anâ’îyat). For that subjectivity is, by its very nature, life, light, manifestation, and self-awareness (hayât, nûr, zohûr, sho’ûr bi-dhâti-hi). All these terms also describe the pure Essences that are separate from matter, whether they are entirely free of it, like the archangelic Intelligences, or charged with governing a body, like the heavenly Souls and human souls. This is not knowledge of a logical universal.

In contrast to the knowledge of abstract universals, called representational knowledge (’ilm sûrî), Sohrawardî calls the first kind knowledge by presence: unitive, intuitive knowledge (’ilm hozûrî, ittisâlî, shohûdî). It is knowledge of an essence in its absolutely real, individual existence, freed from every reference both to logical abstraction and to embodiment in a sensory phenomenon. When every veil has been lifted and removed, and because the soul's being is a being of light, an illumination emanates from the soul: the dawn of its presence (ishrâq hozûrî) upon the object of its vision. From that moment, the soul knows the object because the object itself is present to it and through it—not merely represented before it by a form or an idea. The object is present in its very being. And this presence consists in the soul's “rising” over what is present, making it present through the soul's own presence. Its manifestation is the presence of that presence. This is what constitutes Eastern presence (hozûr ishrâqî): presence at the very East of knowledge.

Yet this power of “making present” (istizhâr) is proportionate to the degree of separation (tajarrud): the degree to which the knowing subject has freed itself from the matter of this world, and thus the degree of its presence at the East, or at the successive Easts. At the same time, this freedom from matter determines the degree of the Dominion of Light over matter and darkness (tasallot ishrâqî). For the soul may descend until it becomes a wavering shadow at evening twilight, sinking into the abyss of what Sohrawardî calls the Western Exile. Presence, then, is proportionate to this Dominion of Light, and knowledge is proportionate to Presence.

We can begin to see why Sadrâ Shîrâzî, whose metaphysics of existing culminates in a metaphysics of Presence, belongs firmly to the “Eastern” (ishrâqî) tradition. We can also see how “prophetic philosophy,” centered on the teachings of the holy Imams of Shiism, led this ishrâqî tradition toward a metaphysics of testimony: testimony understood as the presence of the eyewitness (shâhid, shahîd; see Book V).

Furthermore—and here we reach the heart of “Eastern Theosophy”—it is through this idea of the Dominion of Light, inseparable from “Eastern Presence” and determining the hierarchy of degrees of being and knowing, that a fundamental conception of Mazdean theosophy asserts itself anew in philosophical life: the Light of Glory, the Xvarnah.

When Sohrawardî uses the characteristic expression tasallot ishrâqî to describe the victorious Dominion of Light rising at its East, the dominion revealed at morning, or the term Anwâr qâhira to designate the archangelic order of the overpowering, victorious Lights, we can hear behind the Arabic words the Middle Persian and Persian pêrôz and pêrôzîh. These convey the idea of the victorious one's victory, the power of being victorious (compare the Latin title Angelus victor, given to the Archangel Michael; see Chapter III, § 3). These Sohrawardian expressions all correspond to the manifestations and powers of the Light of Glory, the Xvarnah, celebrated in the Avesta, the sacred book of Zoroastrianism (see Chapter III). Ultimately, it is in this vision of the Xvarnah that Sohrawardî's vision of Ishrâq, of the Light of the East, originates. Its forms of manifestation—the illuminations (ishrâqât)—establish the succession of the dawns and mornings of being.

In an eternal dawn, at the summit of the hierarchy of Light or being, shines the Light of Lights (Nûr al-Anwâr), whose transcendence, whose freedom from matter (tajarrud), surpasses every other immateriality. Its absolute, victorious Dominion (tasallot wa qahr) calls all existence into being: that is, it makes all existence present to itself in an absolute Presence. From this Light of Lights, whose essence is what the ancient Persians called the Light of Glory—the Avestan Xvarnah, the Persian Khorrâh—emanates the first of the “archangelic” or “victorious” Lights (Anwâr qâhira). Sohrawardî gives this first Light the name it bears in Zoroastrian angelology: Vohu-Manah in the Avesta, Bahman in Persian. It is the first of the Zoroastrian Archangels, the Ahmaraspands, or “Holy Immortals.” From the illumination and reflection that constitute the relation between the Light of Lights and the First Archangel, a new Light proceeds: the second Archangel, and so on.

For this original relationship is the source and archetype of all the others, the source of successive irradiations, of the successive Easts of being. Illumination and reflection; the sovereign power of Light and the loving longing that answers it, because the Light itself awakens that longing (qahr wa mahabbat): at the dawn of being, this original relationship is the relationship between the first Beloved and the first Lover. The Power of this radiance beyond the senses holds together the being of every being, arranges all the beings of all the worlds in pairs, and causes the original relationship of love between the Light of Lights and the First Archangel to be repeated endlessly among them. This is not dualism but duality-in-unity, an essential polarity within every being. Beings discover that polarity by being present at the East, at the “morning,” of one another, just as every being is present to the Angel who is the lord of its species.
Thus, from one rank to the next, the whole hierarchy of archangelic Lights illuminates every lower rank with Presence.

Sohrawardî's original and fundamental intuition—the intuition of Ishrâq, of the Xvarnah—already contains within it all the moments through which it will later unfold. What we have sketched in a few lines will be completed and developed in the angelology (see Chapter III, §§ 3–4). This also explains why the expressions of Sohrawardî's technical vocabulary form such characteristic harmonies: Eastern vision; contemplation at the East (moshâhadat ishrâqîya); Eastern knowledge by presence (’ilm ishrâqî hozûrî); the East of a Presence (ishrâq hozûrî). This is a vision that brings about the “morning” of its object, making that object present. For the seeing soul, itself illuminated by the archangelic Intelligence nearest to it, is itself the light of that “morning.” Its knowledge of every “object” is brought back to the knowledge through which it knows itself.

“Eastern Presence” (hozûr ishrâqî) makes every entity separated from Matter, and freed from matter's potentiality, into an East for things and beings, at each degree of the hierarchy of existence. Here is an absolute knowing whose truth no longer depends on any temporal qualification attached to the object—“will be,” “has been,” and so forth. It is knowing in the present, presence itself establishing the specifically “Eastern” relationship (izâfat ishrâqîya) with everything known, known within that very Presence. These are the “Eastern sciences” (’olûm ishrâqîya). And this relationship lies so profoundly at the foundation of both being and knowing that all the terms by which we try to express it become interchangeable and reciprocal: it is the dawn of substance, but also the very substance of dawn; the vision of essence, but also the essence of vision.

This is why “Eastern knowledge” cannot be attained without satisfying a rigorous requirement. Sohrawardî formulates it in a passage so striking that many who followed the tradition of Ishrâq after him quoted it in their turn: Mîr Dâmâd, for example, whom we mentioned earlier, and Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî, both among the greatest mystical theosophers of Safavid Persia (see Book V). Sohrawardî himself appealed to exemplary precedents: the ecstatic vision of Plotinus, which he knew through the so-called Theology of Aristotle; the visions of Hermes and Zoroaster; and the visions of the Prophet of Islam. The passage is the very one to which we referred earlier, where our shaykh traces the spiritual ancestry of the Ishrâqîyûn back to Hermes. After naming those through whom the two spiritual leavens—that of the sages of ancient Persia and that of the Pythagoreans—were transmitted, he concludes:

“In short, the theosopher who truly possesses hieratic experience (hakîm mota’allih) is one for whom the material body has become like a tunic, which he sometimes takes off and sometimes puts on again. No one can be counted among the mystical theosophers so long as he knows nothing of this sacred leaven, so long as he has not experienced the taking off and putting on. After this, he ascends toward the Light if he wishes. He appears, if it pleases him, in whatever form he chooses. The power that enables him to do so is brought into action within him by the Light whose dawn embraces his person (al-nûr al-shâriq ’alay-hi).

“Do you not see how iron, heated until it glows by the action of fire, comes to resemble the fire itself, shining with its brightness and burning with its heat? So too the soul, spiritual in its essence, when it undergoes the action of the Light and puts on the robe of rising dawn, produces the effect and action of the Light. It gives a sign, and the thing occurs at its signal. It imagines, and what happens accords with the image it has imagined. Impostors, the goêtes, seduce people through tricks and sleight of hand.
“But the Illuminated One, the Perfect One, whose love is attached to the order that is innocent of evil, acts with the spiritual assistance of the Light, because he himself is a child of the Light.”

Finally, our shaykh makes an important clarification: these allusions can truly be understood only by reference to the events that take place in the “intermediate East”—that is, in the imaginal world whose reality and ontological status, as we indicated above, Sohrawardî was the first to establish systematically.
3. The Hierarchy of Spiritual Sages and the Mystical “Pole”

When Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî (see Book V) describes ishrâqî spirituality as an intermediate reality (barzakh) that brings together the method of the pure Sufis, directed essentially toward inner purification, and the method of the philosophers, directed toward pure knowledge, he expresses with complete fidelity to the inspiration of the shaykh al-Ishrâq what constitutes the essence of “Eastern Theosophy.” There is, indeed, a form of Sufism that has deliberately set aside, even despised, all philosophical teaching, suspecting it of delaying the spiritual seeker on the way to the goal. And there is a philosophy that has forgotten this goal altogether, contenting itself with theoretical problems. For an ishrâqî, an “Easterner” of Sohrawardî's school, a mystic without philosophical training runs a serious risk of going astray. Conversely, a philosopher who fails to understand that philosophy must blossom into a personal spiritual realization wastes his time in a fruitless pursuit.

Neither of these figures is the intended reader of the Eastern Theosophy. The work presupposes, first of all, a serious philosophical education. Its reader should already have studied Peripatetic philosophy, discussed throughout the works that constitute Sohrawardî's threefold philosophical preparation.

But there is a second condition: the reader must not wish to stop there. The ishrâqî school is neither a Sufi tarîqat, an organized spiritual brotherhood, nor a philosophers' club. It has no need of an organization or archives; nor does anyone belong to it merely by professing this or that opinion. Our authors have traditionally repeated that Ishrâq, “Eastern Theosophy,” stands in relation to the philosophers' theoretical philosophy as Sufism stands in relation to the scholastic theology of Kalâm. This is an analogy between relationships, not an identification of the things being compared, and it conveys the situation particularly well. Someone may be both a Sufi and an ishrâqî, but not because of membership in any particular tarîqat. It is because of a whole lifetime of effort directed toward inner, “esoteric” truth. In this same sense, we shall see Haydar Âmolî (Book IV) explain why there is a Sufism that is true Shiism.

Yet one may also be a Sufi without being an ishrâqî, just as one may be a Sufi without being Shiite—unless, perhaps, one is a Shiite without knowing it. This is why we shall find Sadrâ Shîrâzî, speaking as an ishrâqî, denouncing a certain “obscurantist” Sufism. We shall also find a fully committed Shiite theosopher, a man of profound spiritual experience such as Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î, rejecting Sufism as well. These are some of the dividing lines within the spirituality of Iranian Islam, lines that the present book hopes to help us discern and encourage us to explore more deeply.

The preceding pages have shown us something of Sohrawardî's ideal of the mystical sage; the pages that follow will define it more precisely. We have heard him lament the sadness of his times: the higher sciences have disappeared, and the road to theosophical wisdom has been cut off. He has spoken of his ceaseless search for a companion who would share his love of the higher sciences, and we wondered whether it was possible that he had never found one. He certainly had companions.

But insofar as they were truly his companions—the “brothers” to whom his books are dedicated—they probably shared his pessimism. On the one hand, that pessimism is explained by the conditions necessary for the realization of the complete theosophical sage. The union of philosophy and mystical experience is rare, perhaps exceptional. The relative development of these two qualities in a single person is precisely what determines the hierarchy of the “Sages of God.”

On the other hand, this pessimism expresses itself as a despair that never ceases to hope in spite of itself, because it knows why it can trust in spite of itself. This desperatio fiducialis—to borrow once again Luther's expression, a despair sustained by trust—is not only characteristic of the Shiite spiritual outlook. The reason Sohrawardî gives for it is exactly the reason professed by Twelver Shiism. Here we encounter something more than an affinity: a deep understanding between Shiism and Ishrâqism. It explains why Eastern theosophy found itself so thoroughly “at home” in the hearts of so many Shiite thinkers.

This reason is stated at the very point where Sohrawardî describes the hierarchy of the mystical sages. It appears in the prologue to his great work, in the passage quoted earlier, immediately beside the lines where he sketches the ancestry of the Ishrâqîyûn, the line through which the “spiritual leaven” was transmitted. It is a declaration that, from the outset, quietly undermines the radical pessimism inspired by the ruins of the vanished higher sciences.

“Do not imagine,” writes our shaykh, “that mystical theosophy existed in a period not so distant from our own and has since disappeared. No! The world has never been, and never will be, without mystical theosophy. There will always be someone who preserves in the world its proofs and testimonies. That person is the khalîfe, the representative of God upon this Earth, and so it will remain for as long as the Heavens and the Earth endure.”
This is exactly what Twelver Shiism professes concerning the Imam who is presently hidden: the Pole. To human eyes, everything is hopeless.

Yet because “the matter now belongs to God alone,” pessimism never ceases to overcome itself. The commentators develop this theme at length. They know that around the “hidden” Pole there is an entire group of men who are, in truth, “the pillars that still uphold the world.” It is through them that the outpouring of divine grace continues to reach this world. If an age were ever deprived of them, the world would perish in a final catastrophe. Who are these men? Into what categories do they fall? Once again, we encounter the theme of the esoteric hierarchy already made familiar to us by the Shiite tradition (see Book I, Chapter III, § 4).
Sohrawardî divides this hierarchy into five degrees, with the central degree, the third, forming the summit of the pyramid. We may distinguish five cases.

In the first case, the theosopher, the “sage of God” (hakîm ilâhî), has penetrated deeply and extensively into mystical experience—ta’alloh, theôsis—but that experience is not accompanied by philosophical work. The commentators point out that this was the case with the prophets and with the “Friends of God” among the Sufi shaykhs: Bastâmî, Sahl Tostarî (whose places in the genealogy of the Ishrâqîyûn we should recall), and Hallâj.

In the second case, the reverse of the first, the sage is a master of philosophical speculation but lacks mystical experience. This is the case with the majority of the Peripatetic philosophers who form the school of Aristotle.

In the third case, the sage possesses both perfect philosophical knowledge and perfect mystical experience. The commentators observe that such a person is rarer, and more extraordinary, than the philosopher’s stone or the alchemists’ elixir. They add that this achievement required the technical structure of philosophy to have reached completion, something owed to Aristotle.
Yet among the “moderns”—that is, in the Islamic world—they know of no one before the author of Eastern Theosophy who combined these two forms of wisdom, philosophical and mystical.

There are, finally, fourth and fifth cases. In one, the sage has a sound grasp of speculative philosophy but only middling spiritual experience; in the other, the balance is reversed, with fairly developed mystical experience but limited philosophical training.

To these five ranks of fully initiated sages, or theosophers, Suhrawardi adds three ranks of seekers, aspirants, or beginners. These correspond to the three basic paths into which the first five ranks can be grouped: those who seek mystical experience alone; those who seek philosophical knowledge alone; and those who seek both. The hierarchy envisaged by the theosophy of Illumination thus has eight ranks in all.

Some important distinctions follow. Without question, it is the sage of the third kind who is God’s true khalifa, or representative, on earth. If such a sage is unavailable, to whom does spiritual authority pass? We are told that even a mystic without philosophical training takes precedence over a philosopher who, however accomplished, has no mystical experience. As Suhrawardi and his commentators explain, a minister must receive his appointment directly from his sovereign.

But what claim to such direct appointment could philosophers who rely on reason alone possibly make? How could they vouch for a world they have never truly encountered? How could they answer on its behalf? Suhrawardi himself made clear that he first experienced the realities described in his book and only afterward undertook to justify them philosophically.

In the end, though, the question of succession is theoretical: the perfect sage is never absent from this world, even when hidden from it. Here the Shaykh al-Ishraq, the Master of Illumination, comes so close to the Shiite belief in the Hidden Imam that the religious scholars of Aleppo, who tried him, did not miss the implication.

“In truth,” he writes, “the earth is never without a sage who possesses the highest mystical experience. A sage who was a consummate philosophical thinker but had not entered deeply into mystical experience would, no doubt, have no claim to authority on God’s earth. For the world is never without a sage who possesses the highest spiritual experience, and such a sage has a stronger claim to authority than someone who is merely a philosopher. The office of khalifa, of God’s representative, requires direct investiture.

“But when I speak of the authority (ri’yasat) belonging to the perfect sage, I do not mean the triumphant exercise of worldly power. Far from it! The Imam endowed with sacred mystical experience (al-Imam al-mota’allih) may reveal himself openly and have his authority publicly acknowledged, but he may equally remain hidden. Even then he is the one called the Pole (Qotb), and the authority is his, even if human beings know nothing of him. When power actually rests in his hands, the age is an age of light.
“But when an age is bereft of all divine guidance and ordering (tadbir ilahi), darkness prevails.”

The Shiite resonance of these words is immediately apparent. In the sixteenth century, Mohammad Sharif Harawi, who translated and commented on Eastern Theosophy in Persian, stressed that the authority in question was essentially spiritual (ma’nawi), not an outward authority exercised over the temporal affairs of the visible world.

Shahrazuri, for his part, observes: “Conversely, many of those who actually wield visible power are not even worthy of the name, so wretched are their souls and so boundless their ignorance. How, then, could they deserve the name that denotes authority in its true sense? No: that authority can mean only the realization of human perfection, whether attained through mystical experience together with philosophical knowledge, or through mystical experience alone.”

On the rare occasions when worldly authority did belong to the perfect sage, these were exceptions: in ancient Iran, for example, Gayomart and the blessed kings Fereydun and Kay Khosrow. As for the prophets and their spiritual heirs, our commentators evoke a sacred history that brings us back to the “cycle of prophecy” already familiar from Shiite teachings about the prophets. Every age has had its company of perfected beings, but only one among them possessed the qualities that made him the Pole. Our authors understand that each prophet sent by God was followed by twelve Imams.

Yet neither the group as a whole nor each Imam individually was necessarily known to ordinary people, let alone acclaimed by them. Quite the contrary: “ages of light” have been exceptional. We need not even invoke the sage who governs Plato’s ideal city. That sage descended from contemplation to involve himself in human affairs.

Here the demand is the reverse, and far more radical. It is the entire human community, whose Pole is the Imam, the sage of God, that must rise beyond its present condition to fulfil a destiny lying beyond the horizons of earthly history. From prophet to prophet, the Call has been heard. The interval between one prophet and the next was a time of interregnum.

But now the cycle of prophecy has ended. “Because the age of the prophets has passed,” Qutb al-Din writes in his commentary, “fools and the ignorant seize power in triumph. Such is an age like ours, when religions have lost their strength, disasters follow one another, the paths and ways of wisdom have been so thoroughly erased that not a trace remains, and the ranks and degrees that make up the hierarchy of Intelligence have been abolished.”

Things, it seems, have always gone very badly indeed. Qutb al-Din Shirazi wrote these words in the thirteenth century, the age of the Mongol invasions. Does the person living in “modern times” need any ta’wil—any spiritual interpretation—to read them as a description of the present? Yet their meaning eludes us unless we recognize the time “between times” that Shiite thought about the Imams calls the time of occultation (ghaybat), the time of the Hidden Imam. His role as the Pole is first and foremost metaphysical and mystical.

It follows that he has no need of public recognition. Whether known or unknown to the multitude, the Imam remains the Imam. His imamate does not depend on fashionable opinions, human whims, or human favour. This is a fundamental teaching of Shiism.

Suhrawardi’s text, however, allows two interpretations. One would accord with the view of many Sufis who hold that their khirqa—the ceremonial mantle signifying their initiation as Sufis—derives from one of the twelve Imams. They recognize that the Twelfth Imam was the mystical Pole “in his own time.” After him, they believe, came successive Poles, generation after generation, from a line of Sufi masters whose names and number are known to the initiated. This assumes that the Twelfth Imam, too, departed this world through death. Semnani, for example, seems to profess something of the kind (see below, Book IV).
But despite its apparently Shiite recognition of the Imams, this conception is incompatible with Twelver Shiite belief.

Shiite followers of Illumination, the Ishraqiyun, therefore had to read the passage differently. The Twelfth Imam’s occultation did not result from his death. It remains a mysterious event, which can be imagined in several ways, but every account must preserve the meaning of his continued presence in this world: the Imam is “hidden from the senses but visible to the hearts of his faithful.” When it is said that he dwells in the “eighth clime,” the “middle Orient”—a realm bordering our world and, unlike the higher universes, still in communication with it—this is what is meant. His ways of appearing during the “Great Occultation” cannot, indeed, be understood apart from this eighth clime.

The Twelfth Imam therefore remains the mystical Pole until his return, which will announce the Resurrection. He has no successor and will have none. This remains “the time of the Hidden Imam.” Even when the title pole is applied figuratively to some outstanding Sufi master, the Imam remains the Pole of Poles (Qotb al-aqtab). We should notice how discreet Suhrawardi is here. Nothing in the few lines where he affirms the existence of the mystical Pole requires us to read them in any way that conflicts with Twelver Shiite theosophy.

Around this Pole is gathered the mystical hierarchy of the “Eastern” sages. It is an entirely spiritual hierarchy, unknown to humanity, just as its leader is invisible to human eyes. It is founded on a criterion that cannot be recognized by ordinary observation, but only by the “spiritual senses.” The Imam alone knows its members. No one joins it by selection among peers, by election, or through a competitive examination. The service they render humanity goes infinitely beyond anything we now call “social.”

The human world owes its continued existence to them, yet human beings do not even know it. Because the law governing their vocation is the same, we have already called them, and shall call them again, “knights of the Grail.” For if one of them were to claim publicly a spiritual rank that he might indeed possess in the secrecy of his consciousness—a rank known to the Imam alone—he would lose his power. By announcing what he was, he would, in that very act, cease to be it.

We have encountered the idea of the Pole and the mystical brotherhood surrounding him before (see above, Book I, Chapter III), at the end of the First Imam’s conversation with his disciple Kumayl ibn Ziyad. There the Imam said everything essential. Shahrazuri, Suhrawardi’s disciple and commentator, knows this so well that, when explaining his master’s teaching, he quotes at length the very conversation translated earlier in this work.
Thus the hierarchy of the Ishraqiyun, the sages of Illumination, leads us back to the hidden spiritual hierarchy taught by Shiism. We have already examined its principal sources.

We shall meet this hierarchy again in Ruzbihan, where its members are those through whom God still “looks upon”—still concerns himself with—our world (on this theme, see also Book IV, Chapter IV, and Book VI).

It would take an entire book to assemble the Shiite and Sufi texts bearing on this essential theme. We have already pointed out some of the differences among the traditions describing the structure of the mystical hierarchy; a few are recalled in a note here. Certain connections and resemblances emerge only dimly, in a half-light, and perhaps they will never become clearer.

Consider, for example, an Ismaili tradition reported by Hasan Sabbah, the famous founder of Alamut, which gives the Imam the name Melchizedek. This suggests a connection between Shiite teachings about the Imam and a school of Christian religious knowledge known to theologians as the “Melchizedekians,” whose teachings developed between the third and fifth centuries CE. One can readily see the interest of such a link for comparative research.

Another example comes from Kaf'ami, a Twelver Shiite author of the ninth/fifteenth century, who identifies the Pole with the Twelfth Imam by drawing an analogy between the hidden spiritual hierarchy and the structure of a cosmic tent: the Imam is its axis, the central pillar, and the four Awtad are the pegs set at its four corners, and so forth. This analogy once inspired a learned Zoroastrian theologian to compare the idea of the Pole with its counterpart in Taoism.

In the Taoist tradition, the region around the Pole Star is represented as the dwelling of an “angel” of holiness, and the highest achievement of holiness as reaching the celestial North Pole. The comparison therefore concerns, on the one hand, the numerical and symbolic arrangement of the mystical palace of Ming-Tang, which determines the structure of the Taoist spiritual hierarchy, and, on the other, the spiritual hierarchy described by Shiite and Sufi sources. This comparison becomes all the more fruitful when it brings to light an important figure of Zoroastrian spirituality: the angel Sraosha (Persian Sorush), whose heavenly dwelling lies precisely “on the polar axis.”

From the standpoint of the study of religious experience, this angel of the Avesta may be seen as corresponding to the Pole of Shiism and Sufism. The name of Sraosha, moreover, appears in some of Suhrawardi’s own writings. There is more. Since every species—including every moral or spiritual species—has its own “angel” (Rabb al-nu’), a Shiite thinker such as Qazi Sa'id Qommi, deeply influenced by the theosophy of Illumination, will show, through his analysis of a famous sermon, that the Imam, the Pole, is the “angel” of a “species” called spiritual vigilance (taqwa; see below, Book V).

Finally, we should not omit the mysterious “Order of Philosophers” whose liturgical calendar, ceremonies, and festivals are described in detail in the encyclopedia of the “Brethren of Purity” (Ikhwan al-Safa’). Their choice of the Pole Star as their qibla, the direction toward which they turn in worship, suggests an affinity with the Sabians, and thus with Hermeticism: the “prayer of Plato” and the “prayer of Idris,” that is, of Hermes, recited during the last third of the night.
I can only apologize for passing so quickly over these details concerning the mystical Pole. Even without the space to pursue them, it was important at least to draw attention to them.

What prompted this discussion was the affinity between the doctrine of Illumination and Shiite theosophy. Evidence of that affinity appears throughout the history of philosophy and spirituality in Iran. Let us bring together three particularly telling features.

The first is one we have already noticed: Suhrawardi’s use of the title Qayyim al-Kitab, “the Sustainer of the Book.” In Shiite traditions attributed to the Imams, this title also designates the Imam’s defining responsibility. The expression al-Qayyim appears again in the closing pages of the Book of Elucidations, without its meaning being explicitly explained.

The second appears near the end of that same book, in a series of commands addressed to the mystical pilgrim: “Rise step by step to the family of Ta-Sin; perhaps you will behold your Lord upon the great road along which you are advancing.”

The two Arabic letters Ta-Sin, like the letters Ya-Sin, are among the mysterious, isolated letters that stand at the beginning of certain surahs of the Quran. There are fourteen such letters. They have been interpreted sometimes as names of the surahs, sometimes as a cipher for the Supreme Name of God, and in other ways. Ta-Sin occurs at the opening of surah 27; Ya-Sin opens surah 36, to which it gives its name—a surah recited for the dying and the dead.

Moreover, verse 130 of surah 37 says: “Peace be upon the family of Ya-Sin.” Shiite commentators understand Ya-Sin as a name for the Prophet Muhammad, and “the family of Ya-Sin” as a reference to the holy Imams. Suhrawardi’s commentators, for their part, cite a tradition that identifies “the family of Ya-Sin” with “the family of Ta-Sin.”

Put very briefly, in the spiritual science of letters practised within Islamic gnosis, the fourteen letters placed like a supporting framework at the openings of certain Quranic surahs are “letters of light.” They represent the hidden Spirit, and also correspond in number to the invisible stations of the Moon and the northern signs of the zodiac. The other fourteen letters of the alphabet are “letters of darkness”: they represent the body and correspond to the Moon’s visible stations and the southern signs of the zodiac.

The fourteen “letters of light,” which may be combined and rearranged, thus point to the hidden, inward meaning of revelation—to the Imamate as the inner dimension of prophecy. They form a cipher for the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.” From this perspective, identifying the “family of Ta-Sin” with the “family of Ya-Sin” presents no difficulty. As Shahrazuri rightly observed, Suhrawardi’s command to “rise to the family of Ta-Sin” carries a Shiite resonance. It invites the mystic to join “the perfected Souls who belong to the Family of prophecy”—that is, the Twelve Imams.

The command given to Hermes during an ecstatic vision of the midnight sun—“Climb to the battlements of the Throne”—then takes on further hidden echoes. It too appears in the closing pages of the Book of Elucidations, and brings Hermeticism, Illumination, and Shiism into resonance with one another. Other examples will follow.

The third feature is the person of the mystical Pole, the Hidden Imam, who possesses the only authority that cannot be called into question: the authority of the Spirit. No doubt this idea can be found elsewhere, in other religious and mystical traditions. Certainly it can, and we shall return to such parallels in the pages ahead, for they confirm the idea’s universal significance. We might even say that Twelver Shiite theosophy, in the work of Qazi Sa'id Qommi for example, found in the idea of the Imam the foundation of a general theology of religions.

Seen in this light, how inadequate is the explanation that an unhappy community, having suffered worldly defeat, naturally invented the idea of the Imam and the expectation of his return as a consolation. Such explanations are generally advanced by people who remain complete strangers to the spiritual reality of lived faith. In any case, as we have already asked, how convincing is this explanation when applied to Persia since the Safavid period? Shiism there was certainly not the faith of a persecuted minority.

No: neither Suhrawardi’s statements about the Pole nor Shiite thinkers’ statements about the Hidden Imam depend upon historical accidents. They express an essential truth, a claim that never ceases: the sovereignty of the Spirit alone. As for worldly rule, we have already noted how insistently Qazi Sa'id Qommi reminds his readers that the Prophet Muhammad chose to be a servant-prophet, not a king-prophet. He had no reason to pass on to the Imams a power he had refused for himself.

We can now understand what Suhrawardi intends when he tells us for whom Eastern Theosophy was written. “This book of ours is addressed precisely to those who seek both mystical experience and philosophical knowledge. Neither the philosophical disputant who knows nothing of mystical experience nor the aspirant whose search is not directed toward that experience will find anything here meant for him.

“Indeed, in this book and in its symbols, our discussions are addressed only to the accomplished seeker (mujtahid) who possesses sacred mystical experience (ta’alloh), or at least to the seeker who aspires to it. The minimum required of anyone who would read this book is that he should already have been struck by the divine Lightning Flash, and that the irruption of this lightning should have become a settled habit of his soul. Anyone else will gain absolutely nothing from our book. Whoever seeks only philosophical knowledge, pure and simple, should go and study with the Peripatetic philosophers. This is an excellent and reliable path when one’s aim is rational inquiry alone.

“But we, for our part, have nothing to say to such a person, and nothing to debate with him, concerning the fundamental teachings of Eastern theosophy. No, the undertaking of the ‘Easterners’ (Ishraqiyun) cannot be accomplished without the flashing forth of the Lights. Some of its teachings have no other source than those Lights. So much so that, if these ‘Easterners’ should come to doubt those sources, their doubt would disappear the moment their souls withdraw into solitude from their bodies.

“Just as we observe sensible things and establish how they exist, and then use those observations to build reliable sciences, such as astronomy and others, so we observe certain spiritual realities and, on the basis of our direct observations, construct the metaphysical and theosophical sciences. Whoever cannot make this path his own will have no share in mystical theosophy and will be left at the mercy of every doubt.”

Our shaykh could scarcely be clearer or more explicit in setting out these enduring conditions. Everyone must judge for himself—beginning, alas, with this book’s own editor and translator—whether he has been reckless in attempting to read it! The preceding pages have allowed us to explore the approaches to the “Eastern source” and to learn what qualities are required of those who set out on the pilgrimage toward it.

Suhrawardi has now told those who are not called to this path, without softening his words, that they would do better not to take it. So we must ask how this “Eastern source” revealed itself to him and to others. Here, above all, we shall see how he came to live for himself the spiritual experience of the wonder-working sages of ancient Persia. Many traditions will echo one another. There are crossroads where “companions of the Quest” arriving from different horizons meet.
We shall then see how Suhrawardi, by creating magnificent symbolic narratives, became a mystagogue: a guide leading the initiate toward the “Eastern source.”

Chapter III The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
1. The Light of Glory as the “Eastern Source”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology

We now come to an idea as distinctive as it is fundamental to the religious world of Zoroastrianism. No single word in a Western language can cover every aspect of this heavenly Light of Glory, this “victorious Fire,” which belongs first and foremost to the divine beings of the Avesta, the celestial Yazatas (the “Worthy of Worship”). One aspect of it appears in a visible form—visible in religious images, at least—as a halo or flame: the Aura Gloriae, the radiance surrounding the princes of Iranian dynasties that lie beyond, or outside, our historical chronologies, such as the Kayanids, whom we shall encounter later.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology

The flammula, the little flame or golden battle-standard from which the word oriflamme derives, may also be regarded as a symbol of this Aura Gloriae. This sacred Glory is made visible in the stylized halo that passes from images of the Saoshyant, the Zoroastrian Saviour, into Western depictions of Christ and the saints, Eastern images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and even Shiite Islamic representations of the holy Imams.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology

In Suhrawardi, the imagery is precise enough to attest a direct line of inheritance. Because this reality is alive within him, he claims the wisdom of ancient Persia as the ancestry of his own teaching. He believes himself entitled to say that he has brought that wisdom back to life, without anyone before him having travelled the same path.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology

We have already emphasized that this undertaking did not conflict with spiritual Islam as it has always been understood by the ‘urafa’, those possessing spiritual insight. Far from it: it presupposed their spirituality, and especially their practice of ta’wil, the inward interpretation of revelation, as an exercise in spiritual life. The Prophet of Islam had himself been enabled to participate personally in the exemplary experiences of the prophets who preceded him, reliving the scriptural events that anticipated his own revelations.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology

Consider, for example, his visits to the prophets during the Mi‘raj, his heavenly ascent. From this comes the idea of the “cycle of prophecy” that we have already drawn from the traditional teachings of the Shiite Imams. The Shaykh al-Ishraq followed the same exemplary path. When he extends the privilege of ta’alloh—the experience of becoming godlike, or theosis—to all the “sages of God,” he knows that his own experience has repeated visions personally lived by the prophets and by the sages endowed with sacred mystical knowledge, whose inheritance he deliberately assumes. He refers with particular affection to the visions of Kay Khosrow and Zoroaster.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology

But that preference in no way diminishes the exemplary importance he attaches to Hermes, the ecstatic hero and father of the sage-theosophers. Similarly, when he recalls Plato’s vision of the “Spheres of Light” (more accurately, Plotinus’s vision), he also recalls the Prophet’s vision of the “seventy-seven veils of Light,” an earlier instance of the same experience. The task of uniting this spiritual lineage of ecstatic visionaries presupposes ta’wil, the practice of spiritual interpretation. And it was Islam—more precisely, Islamic gnosis—that placed the resources of ta’wil at the disposal of the Master of Illumination.
